case.case_title: Chandra Kalyanie Perera and Another v. Captain Siriwardena and Others
case.source_citation: Supreme Court of Sri Lanka, S.C. Application No. 27/90, decided on 30 and 31 January 1991

clause.text: Any person detained shall be brought before a judge and cannot be held without legal order.

case_context.legal_issue: Whether the detention of the 1st petitioner was lawful under Article 13(2) of the Constitution, specifically regarding timely production before a Magistrate and legality of detention orders.
case_context.petitioner_claim: The 1st petitioner claimed unlawful detention, alleging failure to be produced before a Magistrate within 30 days and non-compliance with procedural safeguards under Emergency Regulations.
case_context.respondent_argument: The State argued detention was lawful under Emergency Regulations 17(1) and 19(2) for investigation and preventive detention, with orders signed by competent authorities.
key_facts: The 1st petitioner was detained from 29.01.90 under Regulation 19(2) and later under Regulation 17(1) of Emergency Regulations.
She was not produced before a Magistrate within 30 days as required by Regulation 19(1).
The detention order under Regulation 17(1) was signed on 01.04.90 but was not shown to the petitioner until after filing the application.
Detention exceeded one year and was continued monthly under Public Security Ordinance.
No charges were framed against the petitioner.

reasoning.interpretation_summary: Article 13(2) requires that any person detained be brought before a judge promptly and that detention without legal order is unlawful. The Court emphasized the importance of strict compliance with this safeguard. Detention under Regulation 19(2) must be for investigation and the detainee must be produced before a Magistrate within 30 days. Preventive detention under Regulation 17(1) requires disclosure of grounds and informing the detainee of the order. Failure to comply renders detention unlawful.
reasoning.application_to_facts: The Court found the 1st petitioner was not produced before a Magistrate within 30 days, violating Regulation 19(1) and Article 13(2). The Regulation 17(1) detention order was not shown to her timely, and the grounds were not disclosed by the Secretary. Detention exceeding one year was excessive and unlawful. Therefore, the detention was held unlawful and violative of Article 13(2).
principles_established: Detention must be accompanied by prompt production before a judicial authority.
Preventive detention orders require disclosure of grounds and informing the detainee.
Excessive detention without review is unlawful.
Non-compliance with procedural safeguards under Emergency Regulations violates Article 13(2).

outcome.holding: The Court held the detention of the 1st petitioner was unlawful and violative of Article 13(2) of the Constitution and ordered her release and compensation.
outcome.remedy_or_orders: Ordered release of the 1st petitioner from detention and payment of compensation of Rs. 20,000 plus Rs. 2,000 costs by the State.

link_explanation.why_this_clause_matters: Article 13(2) directly protects detainees from unlawful detention without judicial oversight, which was central to the Court's finding that the 1st petitioner's detention was unlawful due to procedural non-compliance and excessiveness.

evidence.evidence_excerpt: The 1st petitioner was not produced before a Magistrate within 30 days as required, and the preventive detention order was not shown to her timely; detention exceeded one year without sufficient grounds.
